name: Licensing Synthetic Media
title: Licensing Synthetic Media
answer: Licensing synthetic media covers the permissions needed to create, distribute, and reuse AI-generated images, video, audio, and text. It includes rights in training data, model outputs, and any real person's likeness or voice that appears in a synthetic work. The field also addresses how a buyer can use a generated asset, whether for advertising, broadcast, or derivative production, and what the model provider retains.

crumbs.name: Rights and Provenance in AI Art

sections.body: Licensing synthetic media covers the permissions needed to create, distribute, and reuse AI-generated images, video, audio, and text. It includes rights in training data, model outputs, and any real person's likeness or voice that appears in a synthetic work. The field also addresses how a buyer can use a generated asset, whether for advertising, broadcast, or derivative production, and what the model provider retains.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on licensing registries, content credential systems, and contract management platforms that attach provenance metadata to a file. Smart contracts and royalty ledgers are used where payments follow reuse, though many deals still move through ordinary media licensing agreements. Model cards and dataset disclosures provide the factual basis for clearing rights before a license is signed.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners first identify the human and machine contributions in a synthetic asset, then map each contribution to an underlying right or permission. They draft license terms that separate training data rights from output rights and from any publicity rights in a depicted person. Provenance records are attached at generation time so that downstream users can verify the chain of permissions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are copyright claims over training data, right of publicity claims over synthetic likenesses, and consumer confusion from undisclosed synthetic media. Licenses often require provenance metadata to remain attached and prohibit uses that impersonate a real person. Because courts are still settling whether model outputs are protectable, many agreements rely on contract terms rather than on a stable statutory right.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Licensing is moving toward machine-readable terms that travel with a file and can be enforced automatically across platforms. Standard clauses for synthetic voices, faces, and styles are likely to emerge as case law clarifies ownership. The near-term goal is a system where a buyer can see the full permission chain for any generated asset before using it.
